chapter_name: The Wild Swans at Coole by W. B. Yeats
learning_objective: 🎯 Reflect on the painful passage of time, aging, and mortality as Yeats contrasts his fading youth with the unchanging, eternal beauty of wild swans!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Yeats visits Coole Park in autumn—a season symbolizing growing old. He counts 59 swans on the lake, just as he did 19 years ago when he first visited.
The poet reflects with heartbreak that 'all's changed' since his first visit. He has grown older, weary, and sorrowful, burdened by the passing of time and personal heartbreak.
In contrast to the aging poet, the swans appear 'unwearied.' They swim in loving pairs, passionate and free, representing nature's enduring energy and timeless beauty.
Yeats wonders where the swans will build their nests once they fly away from Coole Park—a quiet acceptance that beauty and inspiration outlive any single human life.

fun_activity.title: 📸 Then vs. Now
fun_activity.instructions: Think of a park or place you used to visit when you were much younger. What has stayed exactly the same there (trees, lake, sky), and how have *you* changed since then?

exam_tips: 📌 Explain the significance of the number 59: an odd number means one swan is without a mate, subtly reflecting Yeats's own feelings of loneliness and unrequited love.
📌 Contrast the seasonal imagery of 'autumn' and 'twilight' (human decline/aging) with the energetic, soaring flight of the swans.
📌 Coole Park was the estate of Lady Augusta Gregory, Yeats's close friend and patron—the setting holds deep autobiographical meaning.
quick_recap: ⭐ Yeats has been observing the swans at Coole Park for nineteen autumns.
⭐ The swans represent passion, freedom, and art that remain immune to the decay of time.
⭐ The poem captures the bittersweet contrast between human mortality and nature's permanence.
